content: The Grahamites were followers of Reverend Sylvester Graham, a Presbyterian minister and American dietary reformer who lived from 1794 to 1851. Graham was an early advocate of what we might now call alternative medicine, though the term did not exist during his time. His followers adhered strictly to his teachings, which encompassed all aspects of lifestyle. They practiced abstinence from alcohol, maintained a vegetarian diet, engaged in frequent bathing, and generally embraced a minimalist way of living. Graham also strongly promoted sexual abstinence, particularly condemning masturbation, which he believed was a moral evil that could lead to insanity. He viewed all forms of excitement as detrimental to health and prohibited the use of spices in food, considering them harmful. Consequently, the dietary recommendations he proposed were notably bland, leading his followers to consume significant amounts of Graham crackers, a food product he himself invented. Graham and his followers were highly critical of white bread, which they deemed nutritionally deficient—a perspective that has been echoed by advocates of alternative medicine and nutritionists ever since. Some Grahamites abandoned the movement after Graham's death at the age of 57, but others continued to uphold his principles. Beyond the crackers, one of the most enduring contributions of the Grahamites to American culture was their emphasis on frequent bathing, a practice that remains more common in the United States than in many other parts of the world. Graham's ideas later influenced figures such as Dr. John Harvey Kellogg and his brother Will Keith Kellogg, who extended the Grahamite philosophy into their own dietary innovations, including the creation of corn flakes. Grahamism also played a role in shaping the vegan movement. Graham himself believed that meat and dairy products stimulated sexual desires, and he argued that consuming animal byproducts fostered lust. As a result, Grahamism rejected meat, animal-derived foods, and alcohol in pursuit of a purer mind and body. The movement enjoyed significant popularity during the 1860s to 1880s but quickly declined in influence. Today, it is primarily remembered for its association with Graham crackers.
